title: Trickle-Down That Actually Trickles Down: Pushing Anchor-Buyer Credit All the Way to Tier-4
content_md:
# Trickle-Down That Actually Trickles Down: Pushing Anchor-Buyer Credit All the Way to Tier-4

There is more than a **trillion dollars** of unmet trade-finance demand sitting in the global economy right now, and almost all of it lands on the same victims: the small suppliers buried two, three, or four tiers below the brand-name buyers that actually drive a supply chain's cash flow. I spent the last stretch of work building and stress-testing a fix for the precise technical reason that money never reaches them. This post is about what I built, how it works, and the numbers that came out the other end.

## The Credit Cliff Nobody Talks About

Picture a supply chain as a graph. At the top sits the *anchor* — think a global automaker or a big-box retailer. When that anchor confirms a payable to its tier-1 supplier, banks fall over themselves to lend against it. Why? Because the credit risk isn't really the supplier's risk — it's the anchor's. This is the entire basis of **reverse factoring**, a multi-hundred-billion-dollar industry. A creditworthy buyer's promise to pay is the single most valuable piece of collateral in supply-chain finance.

Here's the problem. That collateral **stops dead at tier-1**.

The moment value moves one more hop — from the tier-1 supplier to the tier-2 component maker, then to the tier-3 raw-material vendor — the legal and informational link back to the anchor is severed. The tier-2 SME holds an invoice on its *tier-1 customer*, not on the anchor. So it gets financed, if at all, at its own standalone, often distressed, rate. And that penalty compounds at every tier down.

The result is a cliff: near-prime financing at tier-1, and effectively **no financing** at tier-3 — even though every single tier ultimately depends on the exact same confirmed anchor cash flow.

## Why This Is Hard: The Split-or-Trace Dilemma

The technical gap is sharp and specific. Today's payment obligations are **indivisible** and **non-endorsable**.

A confirmed payable with face value `F` cannot be carved into a `0.3F` slice that a tier-1 supplier endorses down to its tier-2 vendor while keeping `0.7F` for itself. And on the rare ledger that *does* permit transfer, doing it tends to destroy one of two things:

1. **Traceability** — the cryptographic proof that this slice is genuinely a fragment of the anchor's original obligation, or
2. **Privacy** — the confidentiality of the bilateral price, volume, and counterparty terms that every pair of trading partners treats as a trade secret.

Prior blockchain efforts in this space only ever solved *one* horn of the dilemma:

- **Public-ledger tokenization** gives you perfect traceability — and broadcasts everyone's commercial terms to the entire world.
- **Permissioned consortia** (Marco Polo, we.trade) preserved privacy but historically couldn't split credit past tier-1. Marco Polo notably collapsed into insolvency amid liquidity and governance failures.
- **Closed commercial platforms and central-bank pilots** proved deep-tier propagation is commercially valuable — but their privacy and value-conservation guarantees are neither formally specified nor independently auditable.

What was missing was an abstraction that delivers **both** at once.

## The Abstraction: A Splittable Anchor-Credit Token

The right primitive, I argue, is a **splittable anchor-credit token**: a divisible holding whose issuer and signatory is *permanently the anchor*, such that every descendant slice — no matter how deep it travels — is cryptographically a fragment of the same confirmed obligation, while the *act* of splitting and endorsing it is visible only to the two parties involved in that specific split.

I implemented this on **Daml Finance** running on **Canton**, which turns out to provide exactly the substrate this needs. The key property is **sub-transaction privacy**: a tier-3 participant provably cannot observe the tier-1 ↔ tier-2 projection of the ledger, while the anchor's signatory role on the instrument makes every fragment self-authenticating. The anchor is baked into the DNA of each slice; the relationships between slices stay private.

### The moving parts

The token is modeled as a Daml Finance `TransferableFungible` holding, with four core mechanisms wrapped around it:

- **Conservation-enforced split/merge.** When a holding of value `F` is split into `aF` and `(1−a)F`, the contract choice mathematically guarantees the children sum back to the parent. Value can never be conjured or lost — only divided and recombined.
- **A propose–accept endorsement workflow.** Pushing credit downstream is a two-sided handshake. The upstream supplier proposes an endorsement of a slice; the downstream supplier accepts. No one gets credit dumped on them, and no one can endorse value they don't hold.
- **Origination-fee minting.** This is the business model. Every time the platform unlocks financing for an SME that was previously locked out, it mints an origination fee. The deeper the penetration, the more SME financing gets unlocked, the more the platform earns.
- **Atomic maturity settlement.** At maturity, the whole tree of descendant slices settles against the anchor's single obligation in one atomic step — every fragment traces cleanly back to the root.

Because the anchor stays on as issuer and signatory of every descendant, a tier-4 vendor holding a sliver of credit is — cryptographically — holding a fragment of the anchor's confirmed payable. That's the whole trick: **the creditworthiness travels with the slice, but the commercial relationships don't leak.**

## Putting It to the Test

A design like this is only as good as its evidence, so I benchmarked the **cross-tier direct-financing** design against a delegate-financing variant and three legacy baselines: **reverse factoring**, **purchase-order financing**, and **plain factoring**.

The testbed was a Monte-Carlo multi-tier simulation calibrated to the **Dong–Qiu–Xu MSOM model** and **Asian Development Bank** credit-gap figures, run across:

- **200 trials**
- **100,000 tokenized payables**
- **4 supply-chain tiers**

On top of the economics, I ran the security and integrity properties through a gauntlet: **20,000 adversarial privacy probes**, **120,000 double-financing and replay attempts**, and a suite of **12 formal validation gates**.

## The Results

The headline is simple: **deep-tier financing cost converges to within ~30 basis points of the anchor's own cost of funds — at every tier.** The credit cliff flattens into a gentle slope.

| Tier | Spread reduction | 95% confidence interval |
|------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| Tier-2 | **420.1 bps** | [419.24, 420.96] |
| Tier-3 | **718.97 bps** | [717.22, 720.57] |
| Tier-4 | **1072.05 bps** | excludes zero |

Read that bottom row again. A tier-4 SME — the kind of business that today gets financed at loan-shark rates or not at all — sees its financing spread drop by **over 1,000 basis points**. Every interval excludes zero, so these aren't noise; they're real, statistically robust reductions.

And the rest of the scorecard holds up just as well:

- **Penetration depth: tier-4.** Credit reaches all the way down. **100% coverage beyond tier-1** — the cliff is gone.
- **Deep-tier cost gap to anchor: 30.02 bps.** A tier-4 vendor now borrows at almost the anchor's rate.
- **Traceability ratio: 1.0.** Every single slice traces back to the anchor obligation. No orphans.
- **Conservation ratio: 1.0.** Not a cent created or destroyed across 100,000 payables. Value is perfectly conserved through every split and merge.
- **Privacy leakage: 0.0** across 20,000 adversarial probes. No participant could reconstruct a bilateral relationship it wasn't party to.
- **Double-financing successes: 0** out of **120,000** replay and double-spend attempts. The same slice can never be financed twice.
- **Settlement latency: 2.03 s median (p50), 5.54 s p99.** Fast enough to feel instant in a financing workflow.
- **Validation gates: 12 / 12 passed.**

Twelve gates, twelve passes. Zero privacy leaks. Zero double-financings. Perfect conservation and traceability. The economics and the integrity guarantees both land.

## The Honest Caveats

I want to be straight about the trade-offs, because they matter.

This is **simulation-only evidence**. The Monte-Carlo testbed is carefully calibrated to published academic and ADB data, but a simulation is not a live market with real defaults and real human behavior. A default-rate and fee-level stress test does locate the threshold where deep-tier financing stops dominating the legacy baselines — there *is* a regime where the advantage erodes — but inside the realistic parameter range, the design wins comfortably.

There's also a genuine **centralization–privacy tension**: the anchor's permanent signatory role is what makes the whole thing work, and it's also a concentration of authority worth designing carefully around. And a **compute–quality trade-off**: stronger privacy and stricter conservation cost cycles. Those are real engineering dials, not free lunches.

## Why This Matters

Supply-chain finance has spent a decade promising to bank the unbanked tiers of the global economy and repeatedly failing on the same technical contradiction: you could have traceability *or* privacy, splittable credit *or* a verifiable link to the anchor — never all of it together.

By modeling an anchor's confirmed payable as a divisible, endorsable token with the anchor permanently fused into every descendant slice, and by leaning on Canton's sub-transaction privacy to keep each handshake confidential, that contradiction dissolves. Credit propagates arbitrarily deep, every fragment is provably anchored, no value leaks or duplicates, and nobody learns their neighbor's prices.

The payoff isn't abstract. It's a tier-4 raw-material vendor in an emerging market borrowing at nearly the same rate as a Fortune 500 buyer — over a thousand basis points cheaper than today — with a platform that earns its keep on origination fees for every dollar of financing it unlocks. That's a business model and a financial-inclusion story pointing in the same direction.

The trillion-dollar gap won't close on simulation results alone. The next step is a live pilot with real payables and real defaults. But for the first time, the core technical objection — *you can't split anchor credit without breaking either trust or privacy* — has a concrete, measured, auditable answer.

Turns out you can. Here's the proof.
